Molecules have faint polar charges, the most famous, of course, is the dual charged H2O molecule: it has a slightly negative (called delta negative) charge on one side and a slightly delta postive charge on it's opposite side. This dual polarity is what allows it to cling on to positively charged soap molecules and pull them off of your hands while also being pulled from the other side by the negative charges of other water molecules rushing by. In chemistry this tendency of attraction towards the same polar charge is often described as "like dissolves like". You can mix things of the same polarity, but things of opposite polarities will repel each other. Now, when you look at water in a tube, the polar charge of the glass/plastic/whatever molecules are attracting the side of the H2O molecule that is similarly charged, and vice versa, which then causes the meniscus. In fact, if you use a container with a charge opposite of the charge of the compound it holds for example mercury in a glass tube, there will be a reversed meniscus as the two compounds will act repulsively on each other. The size of the meniscus, then, is limited by several things: the force being exerted by the charge of the container on the molecule (and vice versa), the force of gravity pulling the molecules back down, and the friction of the molecule against both itself and the wall of the container that is "pulling" at it with it's charge (also, for added precision, the force that the molecule exerts on itself, ie, it'll be pretty difficult to get something solid to form a meniscus...). K, now, when He is cooled to below a certain temp, it becomes literally frictionless; so now, if put it into a container of similar charge then it will start forming a meniscus but there won't be anything except for the force of gravity acting against it to stop it from climbing higher and higher up the wall of the container. If the attractive polar force of the wall exceeds the force of gravity on the He sample then it will simply keep climbing until it runs out of wall where it's inertia will propel it upward until it is finally overcome by the force of gravity in the air and fall back into the container. This cycle will repeat forever, provided that the He stays below the temperature boundary of it's frictionless phase state.
